readerTitle: Why the plainest slogan in the shop won
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Ronseal, 영국 목재 도료 브랜드) + 실제 연구 (Oppenheimer 2006) + 가상 적용 (철물 체인 PB 상품, 포장재 제조사 전시 부스)
insight: 메시지의 성패는 듣는 사람이 해석하는 데 드는 수고로 갈린다. 재치는 뜻이 한눈에 전달된 뒤에만 보너스가 된다.
misconception: 눈에 띄려면 재치 있는 말장난이나 멋진 문구가 필요하다. 평범하게 말하면 묻힌다.

sources.text: Ronseal brand history: 'Does exactly what it says on the tin' slogan, created with the agency HHCL in the mid-1990s
Oppenheimer, D. M. (2006). Consequences of erudite vernacular utilized irrespective of necessity: Problems with using long words needlessly. Applied Cognitive Psychology, 20(2), 139–156.
철물 체인과 포장재 제조사 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Ronseal 슬로건의 도입 시기(1994년경)와 광고대행사(HHCL)를 브랜드 자료로 다시 확인하세요. 카드에는 'mid-1990s'로만 적었습니다.
이 슬로건이 영국에서 일상 관용구가 되었다는 내용은 널리 알려져 있으나, 사전 등재 여부 등 구체적 근거는 게시 전 확인이 필요합니다. 카드에는 일반적인 표현으로만 적었습니다.
Oppenheimer(2006) 연구 내용(불필요하게 어려운 단어를 쓴 글의 저자가 덜 지적으로 평가됨)을 원문으로 확인하세요. 카드에는 수치를 쓰지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Why the plainest slogan in the shop won
body: In the mid-1990s, a British wood stain brand called Ronseal ran TV ads with no jokes, no puns and no mood music worth remembering.
Each ad simply said what the product did. Then it ended with five words: *Does exactly what it says on the tin.* The line outlived almost every clever ad of its era.

image.label: A plain paint tin on a shelf among flashy cans
image.brief: 철물점 선반. 화려한 색과 말풍선이 붙은 캔들 사이에 라벨이 단순하고 큰 글씨로 된 깡통 하나가 또렷하게 보임. 실제 Ronseal 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Pick the shelf label.
body: You run a chain of hardware stores and you're launching your own deck cleaner. Shoppers walk the aisle fast and compare a dozen bottles.
Which line goes biggest on the front of the bottle?

options.feedback: It might earn a smile, but the shopper has to work out what's inside. Most won't stop long enough to do that.

options.text: "Removes green mould from decking. No scrubbing."
options.feedback: It says what the product is and what it saves you in one glance. You give up charm, but you win the two seconds that matter.
It speaks to a real feeling, but it fits a hundred products. Pair it with a plain line saying what the bottle does.

cards.title: A slogan that became a saying.
body: Ronseal's ads showed a plain man explaining a product: what it does, roughly how long it takes. No metaphors to decode.
The closing line stuck. In Britain, *it does what it says on the tin* became an everyday phrase for anything that keeps a simple promise, often used by people who never bought wood stain.
The brand didn't win attention by being clever. It won by being impossible to misunderstand.

cards.title: Clarity beats cleverness
body: A message works only if the customer understands it in the moment they give it, which is usually a few seconds.

**Clarity beats cleverness** means a line people grasp instantly will outperform a line they have to decode. A pun or a riddle asks the customer to do work. Most simply move on, and the cleverness is never seen.

image.label: Two signs: one decoded slowly, one read at a glance
image.brief: 두 개의 간판 비교. 왼쪽은 물음표가 머리 위에 뜬 채 멈춰 선 사람, 오른쪽은 간판을 보고 바로 고개를 끄덕이며 걸어 들어가는 사람. 간판 글자는 추상적인 선으로 처리.

cards.title: Harder to read, harder to trust.
body: In 2006, psychologist Daniel Oppenheimer gave people pieces of writing in plain or needlessly complex versions.
Readers judged the authors of the complex versions as *less* intelligent, not more. The extra effort didn't impress them. It worked against the writer.
Clever wording often fails the same way. What feels smart to the person writing it can feel like hard work to the person reading it.

cards.title: Clever can work, but only second.
body: Wit isn't banned. It works when the meaning is already clear: a plain headline with a playful line underneath, or a brand everyone already knows.
A quick test: show your message to a stranger for five seconds. Can they say what you sell and why it helps? If not, the clever part is costing you.
cards.softwareNote: Software homepages often lead with lines like "Work, reimagined." A visitor still doesn't know if it's a calendar or a chat app. A plain headline saying what the product does usually helps more people decide to sign up.

cards.title: Clear is not the same as bland.
body: "Quality solutions for your business" sounds plain, but says nothing. Clarity needs specifics: what it is, who it's for, what changes.
And plain words can still be dull. Clarity earns understanding. You may still need a sharp detail or a fresh fact to earn attention.

cards.title: Now it's a packaging factory.
body: You make cardboard shipping boxes. At a trade show, buyers from warehouses and online shops walk past your booth in seconds.
Which banner do you hang?

options.feedback: A pun the buyer has heard many times. It tells them nothing about why to stop.

options.text: "Custom shipping boxes in 5 days. Orders from 500."
options.feedback: A buyer knows in one glance if you fit their needs. You lose the wink, but you get the right people to walk in.

options.text: "Innovative packaging solutions for a changing world"
options.feedback: It avoids puns and sounds professional, but it's empty. Swap the big words for facts a buyer can act on.

cards.title: Say what it is before you say it cleverly.
body: Customers give your message a few seconds. Spend them on being understood.
**Try it today:** take your main sign, headline or product label. Show it to someone for five seconds and ask what you sell. Rewrite until they get it right.
